Dear Corvale Mobility Hiring Team,

I’m applying for the Cloud Infrastructure / DevOps Contractor – Fleet Connectivity role. I’m a QA automation engineer with seven years of experience, including more than two years owning CI/CD pipelines and building test infrastructure for three product teams. I’m now looking to move into DevOps and platform engineering, and the opportunity to help shape infrastructure for Corvale’s fleet connectivity work particularly interests me.

At Odrava Health, I own GitLab CI pipelines used by around 25 developers. By parallelising test jobs, caching dependencies and separating end-to-end execution, I reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly runner costs by about 30%. I also built short-lived application and PostgreSQL environments using Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster. These environments let teams review features before merge and run end-to-end tests in isolation. This work has given me practical experience improving the reliability and operability of systems used across teams, as well as writing documentation that supports onboarding.

I have also built a personal k3s homelab with applications deployed through Argo CD, monitoring with Prometheus, Grafana and Loki, and infrastructure for a Hetzner VPS provisioned with Terraform. My Terraform experience is hands-on but personal-project based; at Odrava, I work at namespace level on a shared cluster rather than administering the cluster itself. I would bring this practical infrastructure experience, along with a QA engineer’s focus on reliability and clear communication, to Corvale’s collaborative, engineering-led team.

Thank you for considering my application. I’d welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience in CI/CD and test infrastructure could contribute to the fleet connectivity platform.

Marta Kowal-Brandt

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is clear, professional, concise, and well structured. It uses credible quantified results, explains the QA-to-DevOps transition directly, and accurately qualifies the limits of the candidate’s Terraform and Kubernetes experience. The strongest evidence is the reduction of pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes, the 30% runner-cost reduction, and the delivery of ephemeral Kubernetes environments. However, the letter remains somewhat general for a role focused on cloud infrastructure, systems design, security, and technical leadership. It could make better use of the candidate’s documented AWS basics, Linux experience, TLS work, onboarding documentation, and mentoring experience without overstating seniority.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The plain-text format is ATS-friendly: standard paragraphs, no tables or graphics, and the role title appears near the beginning. Relevant terms such as CI/CD, GitLab CI, Kubernetes, Helm, Terraform, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, PostgreSQL, and reliability are present. However, AI/ATS screening probability is only moderate because several prominent job terms are absent or insufficiently explicit: AWS, infrastructure as code, system design, networking, TLS, certificate management, stakeholder engagement, and technical leadership. The letter should add only the supported terms and qualify personal-project or learning-based experience clearly. Terragrunt, mTLS, and cloud production operations should not be added because the candidate’s original information does not support them.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The candidate is a credible adjacent or developing match for the role’s CI/CD, Kubernetes test-environment, observability, Linux, reliability, and automation aspects. The letter also aligns reasonably with Corvale’s engineering-led and ownership-oriented culture through its emphasis on owning pipelines, improving systems, and supporting other teams. The principal limitations are genuine candidate gaps rather than writing defects: no Terragrunt experience, no demonstrated production AWS infrastructure operation, no mTLS or broader network-design experience, limited evidence of cloud environment operation, no IoT/automotive or remote-device integration, and no backend/full-stack experience. The candidate’s Terraform is personal-project based and Kubernetes work is namespace-level rather than cluster administration. The letter should present the strongest adjacent evidence while remaining transparent about the transition.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL ISSUES: None. No material hallucinations were identified when the cover letter was cross-referenced with the Original Candidate Information.

IMPORTANT IMPROVEMENTS:
1. In the paragraph beginning “I have also built a personal k3s homelab,” add the candidate’s supported AWS and Linux keywords with an accurate qualification. For example, revise the paragraph to include: “I also have basic AWS learning experience with EC2 and S3 through the free tier, alongside hands-on Linux experience.” Keep “basic” and “learning experience” so the letter does not imply professional AWS operations.

2. In the second paragraph, make the systems-design evidence more explicit by changing “I also built short-lived application and PostgreSQL environments using Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster” to “I designed and built short-lived application and PostgreSQL environments using Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster, with GitLab CI handling deployment and automatic cleanup.” This better matches the job’s systems architecture and infrastructure-engineering language while remaining supported by the candidate’s portfolio.

3. In the second or third paragraph, add the supported certificate-management and observability evidence. For example: “In my personal k3s environment, I configured Prometheus, Grafana and Loki for monitoring, with Traefik ingress and cert-manager for TLS.” This adds relevant observability, networking, and security vocabulary without claiming mTLS experience.

4. In the second paragraph, strengthen the technical-leadership and stakeholder evidence by adding the existing documentation and mentoring facts. For example, after the sentence about onboarding, add: “I also documented the CI workflow for onboarding and mentored two QA interns, helping make technical practices easier for others to adopt.” Do not describe this as formal technical leadership or stakeholder management, since the original information does not establish that scope.

5. In the closing paragraph, replace the generic sentence “I would bring this practical infrastructure experience, along with a QA engineer’s focus on reliability and clear communication, to Corvale’s collaborative, engineering-led team” with a more role-specific version: “I would bring this practical infrastructure, CI/CD and observability experience, together with a reliability-focused QA perspective and clear technical communication, to Corvale’s engineering-led team.” This improves keyword alignment while avoiding unsupported claims about fleet connectivity or production cloud ownership.

6. In the opening paragraph, make the transition positioning slightly more precise by changing “I’m now looking to move into DevOps and platform engineering” to “I’m transitioning from QA automation into DevOps and platform engineering, with hands-on experience in CI/CD, Kubernetes-based test infrastructure and infrastructure automation.” This presents the career transition as a relevant progression rather than an unexplained change of direction.

content:
Dear Corvale Mobility Hiring Team,

I’m applying for the Cloud Infrastructure / DevOps Contractor – Fleet Connectivity role. I’m a QA automation engineer with seven years of experience, including more than two years owning CI/CD pipelines and building test infrastructure for three product teams. I’m transitioning from QA automation into DevOps and platform engineering, with hands-on experience in CI/CD, Kubernetes-based test infrastructure and infrastructure automation. The opportunity to help shape infrastructure for Corvale’s fleet connectivity work particularly interests me.

At Odrava Health, I own GitLab CI pipelines used by around 25 developers. By parallelising test jobs, caching dependencies and separating end-to-end execution, I reduced average pipeline time from 38 to 14 minutes and monthly runner costs by about 30%. I designed and built short-lived application and PostgreSQL environments using Helm on a shared Kubernetes cluster, with GitLab CI handling deployment and automatic cleanup. These environments let teams review features before merge and run end-to-end tests in isolation. This work has given me practical experience improving the reliability and operability of systems used across teams, as well as writing documentation that supports onboarding. I also documented the CI workflow for onboarding and mentored two QA interns, helping make technical practices easier for others to adopt.

I have also built a personal k3s homelab with applications deployed through Argo CD, monitoring with Prometheus, Grafana and Loki, and infrastructure for a Hetzner VPS provisioned with Terraform. In my personal k3s environment, I configured Prometheus, Grafana and Loki for monitoring, with Traefik ingress and cert-manager for TLS. My Terraform experience is hands-on but personal-project based; at Odrava, I work at namespace level on a shared cluster rather than administering the cluster itself. I also have basic AWS learning experience with EC2 and S3 through the free tier, alongside hands-on Linux experience. I would bring this practical infrastructure, CI/CD and observability experience, together with a reliability-focused QA perspective and clear technical communication, to Corvale’s engineering-led team.

Thank you for considering my application. I’d welcome the opportunity to discuss how my experience in CI/CD and test infrastructure could contribute to the fleet connectivity platform.

Marta Kowal-Brandt

critique.content_quality_feedback: The cover letter is clear, professional, well structured, and appropriately honest about the candidate’s transition from QA automation into DevOps/platform engineering. It uses strong quantified evidence: pipeline time reduced from 38 to 14 minutes, runner costs reduced by about 30%, and ownership of CI/CD for three product teams. The explanation of Kubernetes scope, personal Terraform experience, and AWS limitations is particularly credible. However, the letter is only a moderate match for this senior infrastructure-focused engagement. It does not directly address systems architecture, networking, security awareness, stakeholder alignment, or technical proposal leadership. The third paragraph also repeats the personal k3s monitoring experience and could be more concise.
critique.ats_compatibility_feedback: The letter is ATS-readable: it uses standard paragraphs, conventional terminology, and searchable keywords such as CI/CD, GitLab CI, Kubernetes, Helm, Terraform, AWS, Linux, Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, TLS, and observability. There are no problematic tables, graphics, headers, or unusual formatting. AI screening probability is moderate rather than high because several central job terms are absent or only partially represented: Terragrunt, systems architecture, system design, networking, mutual TLS/mTLS, security, stakeholder engagement, and production operation. Those terms must not be added unless supported by the candidate’s actual experience. The ATS value could instead be improved by making the existing evidence more explicit and reducing repetition.
critique.job_alignment_feedback: The strongest alignment is with CI/CD, Kubernetes-based environment automation, observability, reliability improvement, Linux, AWS fundamentals, and clear technical documentation. The candidate also demonstrates ownership across three product teams and practical experience enabling QA and product teams to use ephemeral environments. This supports parts of Corvale’s ownership-oriented and collaborative culture. The main alignment gaps are strong Terraform and Terragrunt, cloud environment design and operation at production scale, systems architecture/system design, mTLS and broader networking, practical security awareness, IoT or remote-device integration, stakeholder leadership across external engineering groups, and production on-call experience. The candidate’s Terraform is personal-project based, AWS experience is limited to free-tier learning, and Kubernetes experience is namespace-level rather than cluster administration. These are candidate-to-role gaps, not defects that can be solved through wording alone.
critique.improvement_instructions:
CRITICAL ISSUES: None. The cover letter does not contain clear unsupported skills or experience when cross-checked against the Original Candidate Information.

MINOR, HIGH-VALUE IMPROVEMENTS:
1. In the opening paragraph, reduce the emphasis on “transitioning” and position the candidate more directly around the supported value for the role. For example, change “I’m transitioning from QA automation into DevOps and platform engineering, with hands-on experience in CI/CD, Kubernetes-based test infrastructure and infrastructure automation” to “My recent work has focused on CI/CD ownership, Kubernetes-based test infrastructure, infrastructure automation, and improving the reliability of engineering workflows.” Retain the transition context later if desired, but do not imply production infrastructure experience that is not documented.

2. In the second paragraph, make the technical ownership and stakeholder scope more explicit using only existing evidence. After the sentence about the ephemeral environments, add wording such as: “I owned this workflow for three product teams and enabled QA and product colleagues to review features before merge and run end-to-end tests against isolated environments.” This more directly supports the role’s expectations around ownership, cross-team collaboration, and bringing users of the platform along.

3. In the second paragraph, replace the repetitive sentence “I also documented the CI workflow for onboarding and mentored two QA interns, helping make technical practices easier for others to adopt” with a more precise leadership and communication statement: “I documented the CI workflow for onboarding and mentored two QA interns, helping colleagues adopt the team’s technical practices.” This is more concise and preserves the supported evidence.

4. In the third paragraph, remove the repetition between “I have also built a personal k3s homelab...” and “In my personal k3s environment...” Combine them into one sentence: “In a personal k3s homelab running across three Raspberry Pi nodes, I deployed applications through Argo CD and configured Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Traefik ingress, and cert-manager for TLS.” This improves concision while retaining relevant observability and TLS keywords.

5. In the third paragraph, make the existing infrastructure-as-code evidence more ATS-searchable without overstating it. Use wording such as: “I also provisioned a personal Hetzner VPS with Terraform and have basic Ansible experience.” Do not describe Terraform as strong or claim Terragrunt experience, because the candidate information does not support either claim.

6. Before the closing paragraph, add one sentence connecting the candidate’s supported analytical and reliability experience to the role: “My approach is analytical and reliability-focused: I use pipeline metrics and test-result data to identify bottlenecks and flaky-test patterns, then turn those findings into practical improvements.” This is supported by the pipeline speed-up and flaky-test dashboard projects and better addresses the job’s analytical-thinking requirement.

7. In the closing paragraph, avoid implying that the documented experience already covers the full fleet-connectivity scope. Change “could contribute to the fleet connectivity platform” to “could contribute to the CI/CD, test-infrastructure, observability, and reliability foundations of the fleet connectivity platform.” This is a more precise and credible match to the candidate’s evidence.
